subsystems.name: Sensor array
subsystems.role: picks up the tiny signals the brain produces during inner speech.

subsystems.name: Analog front end
subsystems.role: amplifies microvolt-scale signals without drowning them in noise.

subsystems.name: Artifact handling
subsystems.role: removes blinks, jaw clenching, swallowing and movement, which are far larger than the signal of interest.

subsystems.name: Decoder
subsystems.role: turns patterns of brain activity into words.
parts: language model to correct and predict

subsystems.name: Compute and output
subsystems.role: runs inference and delivers text on the device.

subsystems.name: Calibration and personalisation
subsystems.role: every head and every brain is different, so the model must be tuned per user.

buildSteps.title: Choose the modality and montage
buildSteps.detail: EEG is fast but spatially blurry; fNIRS is slower but better localised. Combining them trades speed against information.

buildSteps.title: Build the sensors
buildSteps.detail: Dry or semi-dry electrodes avoid conductive gel but need spring-loaded contact through hair; fNIRS needs emitters and detectors placed close enough to reach cortex.

buildSteps.title: Design the front end
buildSteps.detail: Amplifiers must resolve signals of a few microvolts next to mains hum and muscle noise, so shielding and active electrodes matter.

buildSteps.title: Collect training data
buildSteps.detail: A user performs prompted inner speech for hundreds of trials per word or phoneme while their signals are recorded.

buildSteps.title: Clean the data
buildSteps.detail: Eye blinks, jaw tension and motion are regressed out or rejected before the classifier sees anything.

buildSteps.title: Train the decoder
buildSteps.detail: A model learns to map features to words or characters; a language model then turns noisy output into fluent text.

buildSteps.title: Close the loop with the user
buildSteps.detail: The user sees predictions and corrects them, feeding back into per-user fine-tuning.

buildSteps.title: Harden and miniaturise
buildSteps.detail: The lab rig is shrunk into a wearable that survives daily wear, sweat and hair, and keeps raw neural data private on the device.

prerequisites.why: gel-free contact through hair is what makes a headband usable outside a lab.
adds blood-oxygen information that EEG alone cannot provide.
a headband cannot stream raw neural data to the cloud for every keystroke.
imagined speech varies hugely between people, and there is no large shared corpus to train on.
invasive implants in trials have restored speech at near-conversational rates, setting the accuracy bar non-invasive devices must approach.

pathway.milestone: lab systems decoding small sets of imagined words or syllables with subject-specific training
pathway.unlocks: proof that inner speech leaves a readable trace on the scalp.

pathway.milestone: headbands that need only minutes of calibration for a few dozen commands
pathway.unlocks: hands-free control for users with severe motor impairment.

pathway.milestone: generalised decoders that transfer between users with little retraining
pathway.unlocks: a product that works out of the box rather than per subject.

pathway.milestone: continuous free-text inner speech at conversational speed
pathway.unlocks: silent text entry for anyone — and a serious privacy problem needing on-device processing and consent design.
